# IAM: do it

## Ask AWS who you are and read a trust policy (3 min)

<!-- task:start id=iam-t01 -->

Look

**It kills the belief.** "A role has its own password or access key."

> **Cost:** $0.

**Permissions.** `sts:GetCallerIdentity`, `iam:ListRoles`, `iam:GetRole`

**No permission to create resources?** This task is read-only. It needs no alternative.

1. Open AWS CloudShell. Ask AWS STS which principal signs your commands.

   ```bash
   aws sts get-caller-identity
   ```

   Expect: Your account ID and an ARN that names a user, an assumed role or the root user.

2. List the names of the roles in your account.

   ```bash
   aws iam list-roles --query "Roles[].RoleName"
   ```

   Expect: A list of role names. Some names start with AWSServiceRoleFor.

3. Pick one role name from the list as <ROLE_NAME>. Read its trust policy and look for a password or a key.

   ```bash
   aws iam get-role --role-name <ROLE_NAME> --query "Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument"
   ```

   Expect: A JSON document with Effect, Principal and an Action such as sts:AssumeRole. No password and no key.

**Label.** checked against docs, not run in a real account. Checked 2026-10-12.

<!-- task:end -->

## Watch an explicit deny beat an allow (12 min)

<!-- task:start id=iam-t02 -->

Try

**It kills the belief.** "If one policy allows an action, the request succeeds."

> **Cost:** $0. If you forget the cleanup: $0.

**Permissions.** `iam:CreateRole`, `iam:TagRole`, `iam:PutRolePolicy`, `iam:DeleteRolePolicy`, `iam:DeleteRole`, `iam:GetRole`, `iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy`, `iam:SimulateCustomPolicy`

**No permission to create resources?** This command creates nothing. It simulates the allow policy and the deny policy together: aws iam simulate-custom-policy --policy-input-list '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:GetObject","s3:PutObject"],"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/*"}]}' '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Deny","Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/*"}]}' --action-names s3:GetObject s3:PutObject --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/report.csv --query "EvaluationResults[].[EvalActionName,EvalDecision]" Expect s3:GetObject to show explicitDeny and s3:PutObject to show allowed.

1. Create a test role that only Amazon EC2 can assume. The role has no permissions yet.

   ```bash
   ROLE_ARN=$(aws iam create-role --role-name saa-iam-t02 --assume-role-policy-document '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"ec2.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}' --tags Key=book,Value=saa Key=task,Value=iam-t02 --query Role.Arn --output text)
   ```

   Expect: No output. ROLE_ARN now holds the ARN of the new role.

2. Add an inline policy that allows reading and writing objects in one example bucket.

   ```bash
   aws iam put-role-policy --role-name saa-iam-t02 --policy-name saa-allow-rw --policy-document '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:GetObject","s3:PutObject"],"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/*"}]}'
   ```

   Expect: No output.

3. Ask the policy simulator whether the role can read and write an object. The simulator sends no real request.

   ```bash
   aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn $ROLE_ARN --action-names s3:GetObject s3:PutObject --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/report.csv --query "EvaluationResults[].[EvalActionName,EvalDecision]"
   ```

   Expect: Both actions show allowed.

4. Add a second inline policy that denies only the read on the same bucket.

   ```bash
   aws iam put-role-policy --role-name saa-iam-t02 --policy-name saa-deny-read --policy-document '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Deny","Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/*"}]}'
   ```

   Expect: No output.

5. **Predict.** The role now has an allow and a deny for the read, and only an allow for the write. What does each action show?

   Run the same simulation again.

   ```bash
   aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn $ROLE_ARN --action-names s3:GetObject s3:PutObject --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/report.csv --query "EvaluationResults[].[EvalActionName,EvalDecision]"
   ```

   Expect: s3:GetObject shows explicitDeny. s3:PutObject still shows allowed.

   **Why.** AWS [first looks for a Deny statement in every policy that applies](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-deny-checked-first), and [an explicit deny overrides an explicit allow](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-explicit-deny-overrides-allow). The deny names the read and not the write, so the write stays allowed.

6. Fix it: remove the deny policy. No new allow can fix an explicit deny.

   ```bash
   aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name saa-iam-t02 --policy-name saa-deny-read
   ```

   Expect: No output.

7. Run the simulation a third time.

   ```bash
   aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn $ROLE_ARN --action-names s3:GetObject s3:PutObject --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/report.csv --query "EvaluationResults[].[EvalActionName,EvalDecision]"
   ```

   Expect: Both actions show allowed.

> **Clean up:** Run these steps in this order.

1. Delete the allow policy.

   ```bash
   aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name saa-iam-t02 --policy-name saa-allow-rw
   ```

2. Delete the test role.

   ```bash
   aws iam delete-role --role-name saa-iam-t02
   ```

**Verify.**

```bash
aws iam get-role --role-name saa-iam-t02
```

Expect: An error that says NoSuchEntity: the role no longer exists.

**Still costs money if left.**

- Nothing: IAM roles and policies have no charge. Delete the role anyway, so that no unused role stays in the account.

> **Careful:** At twice the stated time, run the cleanup and move on.

**Label.** checked against docs, not run in a real account. Checked 2026-10-13.

<!-- task:end -->

## Watch a permissions boundary cap a role (12 min)

<!-- task:start id=iam-t03 -->

Try

**It kills the belief.** "A permissions boundary that allows an action gives the role that action."

> **Cost:** $0. If you forget the cleanup: $0.

**Permissions.** `iam:CreateRole`, `iam:TagRole`, `iam:PutRolePermissionsBoundary`, `iam:GetRole`, `iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy`, `iam:PutRolePolicy`, `iam:DeleteRolePolicy`, `iam:DeleteRolePermissionsBoundary`, `iam:DeleteRole`, `iam:SimulateCustomPolicy`

**No permission to create resources?** This command creates nothing. It simulates an identity-based policy and a permissions boundary together: aws iam simulate-custom-policy --policy-input-list '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:GetObject","s3:PutObject"],"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/*"}]}' --permissions-boundary-policy-input-list '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:GetObject","s3:DeleteObject"],"Resource":"*"}]}' --action-names s3:GetObject s3:PutObject s3:DeleteObject --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/report.csv --query "EvaluationResults[].[EvalActionName,EvalDecision]" Expect s3:GetObject to show allowed, because both policies allow it. Expect s3:PutObject and s3:DeleteObject to show implicitDeny, because each of them is in one policy and not in the other.

1. Open AWS CloudShell. Create a test role for a workload on Amazon EC2. Its trust policy names Amazon EC2, and the role has no permissions policy yet.

   ```bash
   ROLE_ARN=$(aws iam create-role --role-name saa-iam-t03 --assume-role-policy-document '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"ec2.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}' --tags Key=book,Value=saa Key=task,Value=iam-t03 --query Role.Arn --output text)
   ```

   Expect: No output. ROLE_ARN now holds the ARN of the new role.

2. Set the AWS managed policy AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess as the permissions boundary of the role. This policy allows read-only access to Amazon S3.

   ```bash
   aws iam put-role-permissions-boundary --role-name saa-iam-t03 --permissions-boundary arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess
   ```

   Expect: No output.

3. Read the permissions boundary of the role.

   ```bash
   aws iam get-role --role-name saa-iam-t03 --query "Role.PermissionsBoundary.PermissionsBoundaryArn"
   ```

   Expect: The ARN arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess.

4. **Predict.** The boundary allows reads in Amazon S3. The role has no permissions policy. Does the simulator allow s3:GetObject?

   Ask the policy simulator whether the role can read an object in an example bucket. The simulator sends no real request.

   ```bash
   aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn $ROLE_ARN --action-names s3:GetObject --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/report.csv --query "EvaluationResults[].[EvalActionName,EvalDecision]"
   ```

   Expect: s3:GetObject shows implicitDeny.

   **Why.** A permissions boundary [does not provide permissions on its own](../facts/iam.md#iam-boundary-limits-but-never-grants). The role can do only what is [allowed by both its identity-based policies and its permissions boundaries](../facts/iam.md#iam-permissions-boundary-sets-maximum-does-not-grant). The role has no identity-based policy yet, so nothing allows the read.

5. Fix it: add an inline policy that allows every Amazon S3 action on the example bucket. This policy allows more than the boundary does.

   ```bash
   aws iam put-role-policy --role-name saa-iam-t03 --policy-name saa-allow-s3 --policy-document '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:*","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/*"}]}'
   ```

   Expect: No output.

6. Simulate a read and a write on the same object. Before you run it, predict which of the two actions is allowed.

   ```bash
   aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn $ROLE_ARN --action-names s3:GetObject s3:PutObject --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/report.csv --query "EvaluationResults[].[EvalActionName,EvalDecision]"
   ```

   Expect: s3:GetObject shows allowed. s3:PutObject still shows implicitDeny, although the inline policy allows every Amazon S3 action.

> **Clean up:** Run these steps in this order.

1. Delete the inline policy.

   ```bash
   aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name saa-iam-t03 --policy-name saa-allow-s3
   ```

2. Remove the permissions boundary from the role.

   ```bash
   aws iam delete-role-permissions-boundary --role-name saa-iam-t03
   ```

3. Delete the test role.

   ```bash
   aws iam delete-role --role-name saa-iam-t03
   ```

**Verify.**

```bash
aws iam get-role --role-name saa-iam-t03
```

Expect: An error that says NoSuchEntity: the role no longer exists.

**Still costs money if left.**

- Nothing: IAM roles and policies have no charge. Delete the role anyway, so that no unused role stays in the account.

> **Careful:** At twice the stated time, run the cleanup and move on.
